speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to ask leave of the House to present a motion under Standing Order 43. I present it in the lowest key possible. I want to provoke nobody, and I dare to hope that the government will see fit to accept my motion. Indeed, I have given notice of it to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen).
In view of the fact that we are getting nowhere in batting a certain issue back and forth across the floor of this House, and in view of the fact that the public would like an independent judgment, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters):
That this House requests the government to establish forthwith a judicial inquiry into all matters relating to the escape from custody of Yves Geoffroy.
If the government would like time to think it over that would be fine, but it is a matter that should be settled independently.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is for the government to give consideration to the dimensions of the problem of noise in our society. The time has come to introduce legislation to control excessive outdoor noise produced by surface transportation, it being an environmental hazard involving a variety of physical and emotional ailments including deafness, pain and nervous breakdown.

As a matter of fact, it was interesting to compare the two speeches, which were very different indeed but which at the same time reflected very well the changes which can occur in individuals as they acquire greater experience of this House.
I would like particularly to point out to the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres that of course we cannot keep for many years the kind of naivete which characterizes all of us when we first join this House. Once we become more familiar with the unknown people in this noble institution, once we get to know men better, we become of course both enthusiastic about some things and extremely disappointed with some others.
In this majestic chamber, Mr. Speaker, there is first the institution-the House of Commons itself-which cannot but impress people as an institution, polished as it has been through centuries, and which allows the people, through their representatives, not only to make their grievances known but also to influence the government and the country's general administration. There may be a few things in this area which need to be corrected, but I think that on the whole all Canadians, and particularly members of this House, are proud of this institution which was given to us by the confederation agreement and which we inherited from Great Britain.
Within this institution there are parties and their value as well as that of the men who belong to them vary with time. As for the parties, many things have been said about them both by opposition and government members; they were global and radical statements and the government has been judged once and for all.
I would also like to judge briefly the opposition since it is an integral part of this noble institution known as the House of Commons which can influence the country's administration for better or for worse.
Speaking about the opposition, Mr. Speaker, it reveals a kind of odorless, colourless and congenital impotence. About another party, we might say that it shows shameless arrogance and demagogy and, about still another, that it is an old record always playing the same tune.
In my opinion, the quality of opposition should be enormously improved and we will certainly have this opportunity and no longer hear-

Mr. Speaker, it is quite disappointing for a newly elected member of the House to hear such statements as those made by the member for Prince Edward-Hastings in connection with price controls. Listen to me one moment because this kind of gem is rare.
With regard to price controls, the hon. member stated and I quote:
The second way we can keep prices down is to take steps to keep prices from rising at the very rapid rate at which they are rising at the present time.

There is the whole philosophy of the opposition the co-operation we get from them.
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to stay on that level where, unfortunately, the opposition stands most of the time. Notwithstanding the overall judgment I may have passed on the opposition the fact remains that a large number of the members across the way are worthy men, their hearts are in the right place, they represent their electors honestly and they came here to improve the situation in Canada. It is not because they belong to another party that I underestimate them. Some people are extremely critical of the government and I sometimes find that they are right. Among the most critical is the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Maclnnis) who, when he refers to DEVCO and the issue of industrial development-although, of course, I am not here to make admissions-is basically right and I think that there are some things that must be changed.
What is extremely annoying and frustrating from the opposition is never to have constructive proposals in front of you but to be continuously under the impression that you are on the eve of a general election. The opposition tries by all means to gain the electoral advantages that can be gained in the House of Commons.
At any rate, I shall deal with a more important issue, Mr. Speaker, namely regional development, which was the subject of much criticism here in the House and also outside. This subject is too important for me to season it with jokes or try to minimize its importance by my tone.
Barely three years ago, we tried to launch a concerted attack against regional disparities. We attacked on three levels at the same time. First, we initiated the industrial incentives program. Then, we developed the infrastructure assistance program and improved this instrument which is also used in the agricultural field, namely ARDA. Lastly, we enacted provisions for the social adjustment of workers.
We resorted to these three instruments and tried to trigger a beginning of correction of regional disparities, which has not been successfully undertaken since the inception of confederation in Canada.
Thus, in that first part of the program, that is the grants, my department has accepted since 1969-70, 1,200 applications for grants which brought or will bring about 50,000

new jobs, despite the allegations of some opposition members who should make better use of their research staff. If we take into account the multiplying effect, that will give us 125,000 or 150,000 additional jobs.
Of course it is always possible to retort: there are plants that will go bankrupt, other will not meet their objectives. That is possible, but on the other hand there are other plants which at present expect to employ say from 100 to 150 men, but which will in fact hire 300 or 400 men because their forecasts were to pessimistic.
By the way, those who are interested in research will be able to study what happened under the former industrial incentives legislation and they will find out that in spite of the odd failure the number of new jobs square exactly with the employment announcements that had been made when the inquiries began.
Besides, some cases have already arisen where the number of available jobs has been underestimated and where employment opportunities are actually far more numerous.
Now with regard to infrastructures, Mr. Speaker, we are aware that some regions will never benefit from industrial development if they cannot offer modern enterprise some basic infrastructures. We have therefore entered into agreements with the provinces and this program is now fully operative. It is so effective that we are receiving hundreds of applications from municipalities as well as from various regions and communities in Canada and it has become necessary to create "special" regions in order to perfect these infrastructures.
Here is then a means which, after a couple of years trial has really produced astonishing results.
Then comes the problem of rural planning, farm productivity and development of natural resources. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, we are all aware that thousands of our fellow citizens will continue to make a living out of natural resources and it is our duty, as far as is practicable, to go all out and help them. That part of the program is also very active.
We now have a social adjustment program. Doubtless, Mr. Speaker, when we speed up the urban phenomenon, when we multiply or improve industrial techniques to enable some industries to survive, men are affected. Indeed, they must be transplanted, moved, and all this is part of an a slow and extremely tricky process.
Mr. Speaker, I' remember very well indeed having experienced it one day in Prince Edward Island. We were attempting to convince a farmer to leave his farm to allow regrouping of several of them so that those who would replace him could live decently and use modern equipment. He answered and I quote:

"I was born here, my father was born here and my grandfather was born here. Whatever the government does I am going to stay here".

That is the type of human problems-

Whoever does not care about that does not understand anything. That is why some of the things we do cannot be
February 29, 1972

done overnight. We have to take time, we have to convince people. That is why sometimes, when there are complaints from the other side of the House, I do not think they are serious, because the people over there have never had to deal with such problems. That is why they make such statements.
Mr. Speaker, there has been much censure of the department, in a general way, broad statements, but nothing concrete. I have sought everywhere for some useful information, some meaningful suggestion the opposition might have given us in order to speed up industrial development in Canada. I have tried to understand the New Democratic philosophy in the field of regional development. Well, even young members one might consider to be quite open, such as the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), have, if I remember well-

"You know, policies of regional development have been a complete failure."

That is the subtly distinctive judgment bearing on a whole program, on the efforts of thousands of men, not merely on the federal or even provincial government levels, but on the levels of municipalities and private agencies seeking concrete solutions.
"It has been a complete failure!"
That is all they are able to say after two and a half years of concrete, highly efficient achievements which I shall enumerate later on if you permit it.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I should like to add my congratulations to those which my colleagues have extended to the mover, the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) and the seconder, the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Lajoie) of the address and also to congratulate the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand). I have not seen such a show since the last medicine show I saw when Professor Mulvany was cutting a tapeworm.
Looking over the Speech from the Throne, one is struck by the number of items, some 29 of them, all dressed up with platitudes and folksy words. In the ordinary course of events, were this agenda to be carried out it would take nine or ten months. I note that one of the steps proposed is a program to do more in the way of humane treatment of offenders, with further reforms in the penal system. I want to congratulate the government on this; they did not take very long before putting their preaching into practice. Surely the government will be hard put to it to do any more than has been done for Yves Geoffroy if the stories we hear are correct.
This man was released from prison in order to marry a lady who was a Crown witness when he was tried for murdering his wife. He managed to obtain a false passport and make arrangements to dispose of his property and assets before leaving the country. Is this what is meant by more humane treatment of offenders-if you don't get along with your wife, murder her, it will soon be forgotten? The ad lib women should have a look at this. How do women in general feel about this type of crime? To most men it must surely be repulsive. I am wondering whether this is the thin end of the wedge to distinguish between a domestic crime and other criminal acts.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is what I am coming to. Is taking a life different in a domestic case than it is in any other case?
I do not intend to deal with the Speech from the Throne for too long except to say that if it produces no better results than the preceding three Speeches from the Throne, after which we witnessed mounting unemployment, rising inflation, more people living in poverty and the development of the worst-managed economy in the
Speech from the Throne
western world, the Canadian people will have had just about enough.
When one talks about unemployment one is talking about a tremendous economic factor. When you have 7.7 per cent of the people out of work it is not only that they are out of work but that someone else is keeping them and someone else is paying the shot. It is a tax on the economy and they lose their moral strength and their dignity. The psychological effect on the unemployed and their families may be devastating indeed. This is only a small part of the economic picture when you consider we are losing approximately $3.5 billion in production per year. I do not believe that Canada or any other country can really stand such a situation.
Businessmen have been afraid to invest. Many businesses have been sold. They are distrustful of the government, of the changes in the labour laws, the Unemployment Insurance Act, the proposed competition legislation and of the arrogant use of power in Ottawa. We have witnessed the flight of a great deal of capital from Canada over the last few years and the next year is likely to see a further cut in business.
Last night the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) spoke about social justice. The present government has frozen old age pensions at $80 a month. Let hon. members not forget that the $80 of last year purchases just over $75 worth of goods this year. This situation applies to every pensioner, even those who pass the means test and receive the guaranteed income supplement. The only increase they receive is 2 per cent. That is the social justice that this government talks about!
In one year alone inflation increased nearly 5 per cent, yet we are shortchanging all pensioners in Canada on fixed incomes. Year by year they become poorer. The government talks about economic security, but what about drug care? I think it is worth repeating that the old age pensioner has paid for his pension. It is not a case of their receiving charity; they have been taxed for their pensions and deductiops made from their pay cheques. A pensioner who happens to fall just short of qualifying under the means test is finding that his $80 is being rapidly eroded. If inflation continues at the present rate, which is almost 5 per cent a year, it will mean, Mr. Speaker, that by the year 2000 we will require a salary four times what we have today in order to retain the same purchasing power.
Whether or not inflation and unemployment can be solved by this government remains a mystery. The government has shown no capability for coping with the situation even though it has been in power for four years. In the first place the government has taken more and more tax dollars and has spent more and more. The operations of the office of the Prime Minister alone indicate this; his office has increased its expenditures almost ten times.
I was struck by what Mr. Bennett, the Premier of British Columbia, the so-called bigot of British Columbia, had to say in this regard. He pointed out that the federal government and other provinces had spent extravagantly on the furnishing of government offices and increased their hirings of staff much more so than in British Columbia.

February 29, 1972
Speech from the Throne
The estimates for 1972-73 are up by 10 per cent. This probably means that when the supplementary estimates have been added the increase will be 12 per cent or more before the year is out. It is recognized that government is growing larger and larger. This is true of governments in general, but is probably more the case with the federal government than with any other government. The federal government should at least set an example. Instead it has become larger, more bureaucratic and more inefficient, with little or no knowledge of the people in the hustings who have to work and pay all the bills. It is quite apparent that if the government does not change its direction we are in for very serious trouble.
Today there are more young educated people than we have ever had in this country. But we also have more young educated people without jobs than we have ever had, which represents a tremendous waste of manpower and brains.
Sometimes I wonder just what advice the government receives. The Minister of National Health and Welfare spoke in the House the other day about how deeply concerned he was over the non-medical use of drugs and then-effect on society. Then he went on to say that the government was taking action to restrict the use of two types of drugs, the abuse of which had been a public health problem in this country. I refer to methadone and amphetamines. If a little research had been done or a few questions asked of the medical profession, the minister would have discovered that during the last five years doctors have cut use of amphetamines in half, that during the last half of 1971 use had been cut by more than half. Use of this product has been diminishing very fast. In other words, the medical profession has been policing itself. But no, the government had to interfere.
The point I am making is that the minister is only touching the tip of the iceberg, not the part that lies below the surface. The minister should be tackling the problem of drug peddling and other forms of abuse. This is an area he has not touched at all; instead he had to enter the medical field. In spite of the very satisfactory decline in the use of the drug, the government must use the big stick.
In my opinion the minister has taken a very disturbing step. From now on the ordinary practising physician will be unable to prescribe this drug even though, as a result of his training and experience, he feels in all conscience it should be prescribed. He will now have to consult another physician, which in remote places itself creates a problem because doctors are in short supply. How will physicians in such areas be able to get in touch with other consultants? Not only this, but the minister's action, in my opinion, casts a shadow on the competency of the general practitioner who is the backbone of the medical profession.
When I listened to the minister last night expressing his concern I almost shed crocodile tears. Having heard him speaking about drug abuse the other day, I think the people of Canada would be amazed if they looked at the 1972-73 estimates, which were tabled in the House last Wednesday, and found that the government was going to spend $358,000 less on its drug abuse campaign than it spent last year. On the other hand, it has doubled its anti-smoking program to $386,000 but has done very little about it. So when the minister speaks in those terms it

makes me question his sincerity. Perhaps he was speaking out of both sides of his mouth.
In his announcement the other day I noticed he referred to the Le Dain commission but he did not mention use of alcohol which the Le Dain commission said was the worst drug of all. It was pointed out by the Le Dain commission that there are over 500,000 alcoholics in the dominion of Canada. I see the Minister of Justice in the House. No, I am sorry, he is not Minister of Justice any more; he has been moved up, and I congratulate the minister on his new appointment because he is a great guy.
As I was saying, there are 500,000 alcoholics in Canada. Since 1951 the drinking of alcoholic beverages has more than doubled. Liquor has become part and parcel of our social life. Many people are able to enjoy a drink and have never any medical problems. However, last year there were over 2,000 deaths in Canada from automobile accidents where alcohol was a related factor. This amounts to over two million man-days lost, costing the economy $40 million.
I am not going to refer to any of the diseases caused by alcohol consumption; they are many and are increasing rapidly, and they are mostly fatal. The point I am making is this: How much money is the government prepared to spend to educate our young people to the dangers presented by the use and abuse of alcohol which, according to the Le Dain commission, is far more dangerous than drug abuse? What is the government doing to assist the young people to adapt themselves realistically to a society which accuses them of using drugs while their parents use alcohol and give them the right to drink at 18, even though the minister cannot enforce a law- and nobody is asking him to-to abolish alcohol as he tried to do with some drugs such as the sugar substitutes?
I hear the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) making some remarks. If he wants to stand up and give us his thoughts, that is all right.
What has the minister done about research into this matter? I am sure the hon. member will support me on this. If he sits and listens he will learn. Surely the minister can do something about research into the dangers of the excessive use of alcohol. The danger not only includes harm to the persons themselves but to other people as well because an alcoholic affects the lives of many others. Fortunately we now regard alcoholism as an illness which should be treated, and more research into alcoholism should be carried out. We should spend more money on research so as to prevent the long list of tragedies that follow in its wake.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

This is not the only area in which the minister lags. He has done little or nothing, even though a Liberal government brought in medicare in 1966, to provide the necessary doctors to carry out the increased work required under medicare and to meet the loss of doctors. Last night the minister said in the House that Canada had one of the highest ratios of doctors to population in the western world. I do not like him to mislead the Canadian people and to put the doctors of this country in a bad
February 29, 1972

light, because that is exactly what he is doing. He is not telling the truth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have here United Nations figures which I will table. They show that in Canada we have one doctor per 890 people. In the United States there is one doctor for every 650 people, in England and Wales one doctor for every 860 people, in Northern Ireland one doctor per 780 people, in Scotland one doctor for 780 people, in Sweden one doctor per 850 people, in West Germany one doctor per 650 people, and in the U.S.S.R. one doctor for every 430 people. The World Health Organization figures show that in Canada there are 120 doctors for every 100,000 people, in the United States there are 130 doctors, in the United Kingdom there are 147 doctors, in France, 154 doctors, in West Germany, 193 doctors, in Israel, 250 doctors, and in the U.S.S.R., 250 doctors per 100,000 population. Eastern Europe which fell so far behind has caught up today and they have a better record in many cases than Canada.
I will table this information because I think the minister should stop this nonsense of saying we have the best record in this respect when this is not so. He is casting a reflection on the doctors of this country. The figures which I have read will appear in Hansard.
The government was to provide medical complexes and to provide teachers and equipment to expand medical schools. What has the minister done in this respect? Year after year we have asked for medical schools to be operated in the summer months so as to step up the graduation of doctors by 30 per cent. What has the government done in this respect? Not one solitary thing. Year after year the minister has been promising to see his colleagues about it, and year after year doctors are left shorthanded and are criticized because there are not enough of them to do the work they are called upon to do.
I remember the time in the House when the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), who was the premier of Saskatchewan for many years, said that medicare would increase the workload by approximately 25 per cent. The Hall Commission report recommended that the government get busy at once and increase the number of medical students thus increasing the number of doctors to meet the increasing demands. What has happened? We have only to look at the sorry record. We are importing as many doctors as we are graduating students; about 1,000 doctors were brought into Canada and 1,000 students were graduated with little or no improvement in the situation. A start was to be made at once. We have rejected many of our own students while accepting doctors from other parts of the world who were less well educated that our own. Now the government is talking about medical assistants, about felchers, or whatever you want to call them, who are partially trained doctors or nurses. Would they make house calls? Some three years ago when I was in Washington I was advised by some Russian doctors that they have found the felcher system to be wasteful. The system did not work out so well and sometimes it created problems which took longer to clear up than if qualified doctors had seen the patient in the first place.
Speech from the Throne
The situation we have today has been created as a result of the fact that the emergency units of the hospitals are overcrowded. Many of the units have workloads requiring several doctors and nurses to operate them on an emergency basis. It is grossly unfair to blame the doctors for sloppy work. Their workload has been extended to the point where it is difficult for them to spend the necessary time on a patient or to do a thorough clinical examination, and consequently cases are missed and patients are often seen hurriedly, which leads to expensive medicare. Again and again we find that it is the poor who are suffering and it is they who are going to emergency units in far greater numbers than others. If we look at the record of admissions to hospitals we see that there are three or four times as many poor and underprivileged as there are well to do people.
I was interested to hear the minister say last night that the department would set up clinics to practise preventive medicine. May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, before the noon adjournment I was mentioning the shortage of doctors. To recapitulate, I point out that national medicare was introduced by the parliament of Canada. Once that was done, it became the responsibility of parliament to see that sufficient doctors were provided to implement the findings of the Hall Commission report which formed the basis for medicare. But in the intervening years, no real attempt has been made to provide sufficient doctors.

Speech from the Throne
We need at least 2,000 more physicians per year to maintain the current level of health services, and the current level is inadequate. This does not take into account the number of physicians who go into administration, do research, or undertake the education of other doctors. We must also keep in mind the fact that approximately 50 per cent of our physicians are only in general practice. To illustrate how we are meeting the need, I point out that last year we graduated 1,152 new doctors, but we needed 2,000. I see the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle) looking at me when I say this because he knows that we imported another 1,113 doctors, a lot of whom came from countries that could ill afford to lose them, and from countries whose requirements for entrance to medical school are lower than the requirements of Canadian medical schools.
Furthermore, I point out that only four out of every ten students who applied were accepted for Canadian medical schools. It is not a question of our having insufficient numbers to enter medical schools. I repeat that only four out of ten were accepted. The reason for this was that the government did not provide the necessary health resources fund to make available the spaces and the universities to train all the students we should have taken. That is the real problem. Neither did the government give the universities or students the money and facilities to continue their training during the summer semester.
The health resources fund must be expanded to cope with all the students who wish to go into medicine. Some of those in government and universities say that doctors cannot be adequately trained in such a way, but I point to our performance during the last war. The doctors who at that time finished their courses in four years have not taken second place to any who were trained under the six-year plan, either before or since then. Those who graduated after four years had put in the necessary hours of training. Last year 600 Canadian students possessing all the basic qualifications adequate to go into medicine were rejected, yet I repeat that we accepted 1,100 immigrants from outside the country. In actual fact, we turned down our own Canadian boys and girls. I repeat that 50 per cent of our doctors specialize, or engage in administrative insurance and other fields.
I now wish to deal for a few minutes with the bureaucracy that has crept in under the national medicare plan as a result of the number of forms used. Forms have become very important and when patients are transferred from one place to another these forms have to be filled out in duplicate. I am sure the hon. member for Hull will substantiate this. I have been told by doctors in practice, as he is, that 10 per cent to 20 per cent of their time is spent just filling out forms. This adds to their expenses and leaves them less time to practise medicine. People are getting a little bit fed up with this situation.
In the province of Ontario it costs the taxpayers around $50,000 to train a doctor. People are saying it is easier to get their car serviced than it is to get medical service. Surely, that situation has to be corrected. The high-sounding platitudes spoken by the minister last night are not going to solve the problem. What has been accomplished in his four years as minister? Let him state just one thing

that has been achieved in this field. He talks about community clinics but if there are not enough doctors now to look after the sick, who is going to staff the community clinics? How does he propose to set them up and to service them? I agree with the principle of preventative medicine, but where are we going to get the doctors to put it into practice. Is the minister going to have these doctors on duty every hour of the day and let all the people who are too ill to go to a clinic die without any attention? He says there is too much treating of the sick in hospitals already, so what is he going to do when there are not enough doctors to discover and treat incipient disease. He has not prepared for that day as was recommended in the Hall commission report.
This government stands condemned at the bar of justice for what they have done to the medical profession by not supplying more doctors and for what they have done for the people of Canada under medical care by not providing the doctors to give adequate medical care, either for sickness or prevention.

Mr. }oseph-Philippe Guay (St. Boniface): Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. members for Bruce and Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Whicher and Mr. Lajoie), who performed their task with great intelligence and integrity.

Mr. Speaker, the accomplishments of the government speak for themselves and many members on the government side have referred to them in the last few days, particularly since the Speech from the Throne, so I feel there is no need for me to reiterate at the moment. However, I shall do so in my own constituency because I believe that the people of Canada should be well informed at all times. Statements about events can certainly be slanted so badly by members of the opposition that I believe we have a responsibility to go back to our constituencies and put the record straight by telling our constituents how things are in a straight and orderly fashion.
After listening to the speech of the hon. Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), I should like to congratulate him. Not only did he give the true story of what has taken place in his department, but he also gave the true explanation of what is taking place in various parts of Canada with regard to development, particularly in the DREE areas.
On the other hand, the members of the loyal opposition since 1968 have done nothing but criticize government policies. In all fairness, I must agree that it is the role of the opposition to criticize but what has the loyal opposition offered as concrete, sensible suggestions? Most of the time they talk about doom and gloom-the same old story, the same old speeches. If you took their speeches from one day to the other, put them all in a bag and mixed them up and then took out the words one by one you would get a repetition of the same old thing.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
February 29, 1972

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There has been no change since 1968; in fact, there has been no change since 1962-63. They are still talking about the short time when they were the government. I think they are still dreaming about it and are not doing the constructive job that they should as the loyal opposition. They rearrange their speeches, possibly with a few more words, but they all have the same meaning, the same criticism, the same lack of feasible suggestion.
As an example, let me refer to their own convention held last December 5, 6 and 7 at the Chateau Laurier. I have here a few notes extracted from the various reports and papers. The subject of prime interest to the delegates was Canada's economic independence, the guaranteed annual income, tax bill C-259 and auto-determination for Quebec, but the delegates were so mixed up, Mr. Speaker, they did not know which way they were going. The delegates were not of one mind, the story went, about whether anything at all needed to be done about the extent of foreign ownership of the economy. It was also fairly clear that more of them supported a moderate form of economic nationalism. For example, the first resolution on Canadian economic independence stated that the federal and provincial governments should take urgent steps to reach a consensus on long-term economic and political independence in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to an article published in Le Soleil, the only French-language newspaper in British Columbia. The few lines I have here reflect the feelings of the Francophones not only in British Columbia, but throughout Canada and more particularly in western Canada.
Here is what they say:
The attitude of the provincial government toward French Canadians must change, and the best time for it is now.
The general public in British Columbia seems to worry about the fact that their premier was described as he appears to be; that reaction is unfortunate and somewhat exaggerated when the incident is seen in context. The general public should worry instead about the discrimination against an official minority in the province, discrimination that starts in the very denial of the existence of that minority. We can start remedying this situation by promoting adequate teaching in and of French in our schools, and by supporting rather than hampering the efforts of existing French Canadian institutions and their culture in British Columbia.
Mr. Trudeau has drawn public attention on the well known fact that the government of British Columbia is working very hard to hamper anything French. Let us note the fact that so far, nobody has yet rejected the charge that the head of the provincial government is following a course which seems based on ignorance and narrow-mindedness. The people around him justify his attitudes and policy despite their lack of soundness.
Speech from the Throne
He maintains that French Canadians-the one million of them outside Quebec and more particularly the 90,000-odd in British Columbia-have no right outside Quebec and must accept that.
It can certainly be recognized that it is increasingly urgent and essential that French Canadians be entitled to their language and their culture throughout Canada-even in British Columbia-or else we are going toward fragmentation of our country.
So far, extremists, whether English- or French-speaking, have not been successful in dividing us and they will not sunder us if moderate men are sufficiently anxious to work against any policy of division or discrimination which might exist in our province.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to keep on quoting the article of the same paper:
In order to clarify any misunderstanding, let us mention that there are close to 90,000 French Canadians living in British Columbia, and more than one million outside Quebec, in the nine other provinces.
To put everything into perspective, six of the Canadian provinces have fewer than one million inhabitants, so the million of French Canadians outside Quebec is an important group indeed.
The federal policy on bilingualism is undoubtedly favourable to Quebec and a critical factor for the survival of French Canadians outside Quebec.
Bilingualism is of primary importance for the 1,000,000 Frenchspeaking Canadians residing outside Quebec, and no anti-Quebec sentiment should enter the discussion merely to justify an anti-French-Canadian policy in British Columbia.
That province's government does not provide adequate opportunities for the teaching of French, either to French Canadians or to English Canadians, and an anti-Quebec feeling can no longer justify such a deplorable situation.
If Premier Bennett is not a bigot, let him prove it through his policy, because it is only through this that we will be able to judge.

I think that really tells the story of how people feel. This editorial was written by a Francophone in British Columbia. The same applies to other Francophone groups in western Canada, including Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta where they are certainly numerous. I deplore the fact that after having voted for unity and bilingualism in Canada, some members of the loyal opposition make statements that are contrary to the principles they have supported. In fact, this is evident from what they have said in the past few days. The members of the opposition should either put up or shut up. They should tell the Prime Minister, if they accept his challenge, what they would do if they formed the government. Then, they might make a valuable contribution to proper legislation being passed in this House. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said that this was a forum in which to discuss policies and all kinds of problems. I think it is also a responsibility to come up with something that is sensible. They should make sensible suggestions and not just speak for the sake of speaking.
I would like to speak briefly about something which has been on my mind for a long time, the old age pension. I do not always agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), but I somewhat agree with his philosophies in this regard. I will support an increase in the old age pension. I would certainly be pleased if this came about and I will make personal representations to the government in that regard. I will make every attempt

Speech from the Throne
to do so when the occasion arises. Rest assured that I will do this. I can speak just as loud in caucus as I do in the House.
There is one further thought I have. I would suggest to the government that a lot of consideration be given to the implementation of wage and price controls. I am one who believes that the sooner this is done the better it will be. There are many other things I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members. Perhaps I shall have a chance to do so later on. I shall finish up by saying to the Leader of the Opposition that the sooner he accepts the challenge of the Prime Minister, the sooner I shall take my hat off to him.

Many members opposite who groan will be groaning on election night because they will not be here. Everywhere in our country, men and women of all political faiths, are asking: Where are we going? They have a deep sense of fear. There is none of that pride in Canadianism which has been ours throughout the years, and which was shown to all the world at Expo '67 which my government had the honour to bring about.
I see parliament. What is it? A caricature of the institution it should be. The Prime Minister yesterday made a statement in this House indicating peevishness, pettiness, with profanity. That observation will, I am sure, have the same effect as the short statement by the Right Honourable Mackenzie King in 1930 had on the Liberal party of that day. As I go across the country, I meet older Canadians as well as the youth of our nation. I have always been very proud of them and I am more so with the passing of days. They want to do something for Canada. There are about 4 per cent who want to create trouble, but the rest are motivated by tremendous dedication to the building of Canada. They want to bring about changes and bring them about by democratic means. They come here and they sit in the galleries of the House of Commons. And they leave asking: What manner of institution is this?

The hon. member who preceded me said that Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition did not have the regard for the Queen and for the monarchy that we should have. I find it difficult to understand that anyone could be suffering such a degree of innocence as was displayed by the hon. member in those words. The subject of Her Majesty the Queen has come to the fore with the approach of the election. She was left out of the Speech from the Throne in 1969. The Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), who has the custody of the Seal of Canada, voted for the abolition of the monarchy. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) did the same. The Prime Minister was asked whether he had voted and he said he had not. But he went on to explain that he had less regard for the monarchy than he had for skiing or even for snowshoeing.
Just follow the peregrinations of this government. One day the monarchy is condemned. The next, the Speech from the Throne refers to the fact that the Governor General is thanking parliament in the name of the Queen. A little later on in that speech, Her Majesty becomes "Our gracious Queen". So it is in almost every field, with the Prime Minister making statements one way today and then saying the very opposite tomorrow. That tortuous course was suggested 500 years ago by Machiavelli, who said, in effect, let the people understand what you are doing and you will encounter difficulties. Parliament is one day lauded to the skies by the Prime Minister and the next day members of the House of Commons are described as nobodies. This institution is the only place in which the freedom of the country can be maintained and continued; there is no other.
Now, there is a great national movement underway to build up the Prime Minister. I read that the president of the Liberal Association, Senator Stanbury, said: "We have to build him up". Then, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey) uttered some immortal words. I am sorry to see he is not here today as a result of circumstances that I hope turn out favourably, but quoting him-because, after all, he is worthy of quotation-he said: "Greater faith must be built in the Prime Minister". That shows that some of the Liberals are beginning to need that inculcation. He said he was tired of hearing that the Prime Minister had feet of clay. Only deities do not, Mr. Speaker.
Today in the city of Ottawa there are a number of United States press and radio men who have been brought here for the purpose of seeing the Prime Minister at first hand. Many of the papers of these representatives have agents in the press gallery, but that is not good enough. Do you know the reason they are here, Mr. Speaker? It is because the Prime Minister is trying to make the United States forget the fact that when he was in the U.S.S.R. he said: "We fear the United States culturally"-and I can understand that-"and we fear the United States economically"-and I can understand that. Then he said: "yes, and even militarily". I say there never was a more dastardly statement made of the United States anywhere, any time, by any person. That is why their newspapermen are here today, for the purpose of learning at first hand that the exact opposite of what was said is the truth.
February 29, 1972

I have a great admiration for adroitness, providing it is accompanied by truthfulness. I have been watching the Prime Minister in action and have heard him say one thing and then the very opposite. I often think as I watch him in action that he epitomizes the game we used to play as boys called fox and hounds, in which the fox scattered the paper around indiscriminately in order to deceive those who were the hounds, to mislead them. That is what is happening here.
The cabinet has been shuffled around. The Prime Minister took the deck and shuffled it. He added one that added nothing and shuffled the rest. I have played cards from time to time but have never known anyone, however often he shuffled, who could turn four deuces into four aces. I allow my hon. friends opposite to place themselves or their colleagues in the particular categories.
We have today a cabinet that is noted for its absenteeism, not for good reason but just to avoid having to answer questions. However, there is one minister for whom I have a great deal of admiration, and I refer to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand). I knew him before he became a Liberal, at the time he was a labour leader. Today, he is a minister of the Crown. Can you conceive of a minister of the Crown, Mr. Speaker, with hundreds of millions of dollars to expend, being the leader of his party in the province of Quebec, sending out over his own signature requests for Liberal party funds? Here is what his letter said, in part:
Funds must be available so that the work of the party, in the next few months, may be adequately financed.
This is a course of action that is dangerous to parliament and is something that cannot be condoned. It must have been approved by the cabinet or it would not have been done, and indicates the degree to which this government by insidious methods will place many companies in the position where they will have to contribute, or at least will find that to contribute will be conducive to receiving contracts. Such a course is inexcusable, reprehensible, and cannot be justified in any way.
Since the hon. gentleman who preceded me dealt with the subject, may I too, refer to the Queen. We all know what the government has done with the coat of arms. Only a few ministers have the coat of arms on their letterheads today. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) has part of a flag with a tractor going through it. I do not know whether it is an imported tractor, but it indicates an attitude of mind on the part of all. Although the Prime Minister has not yet removed the coat of arms, others have.
The abolition of the monarchy, may I mention, was in the minds of the Liberal party on December 13, 1968. After all, there was criticism from the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), who is always going around with a scholastic egotism which I like to watch. He now has control over the CBC. I do not know whether he has control over that other gentleman of the Cite Libre, Mr. Gagnon, but I intend to deal with him shortly since his past record qualifies him in every respect for consideration.
Let me quote from Time magazine for the date I mentioned in 1968:
Last week, thinking aloud in the Liberal caucus, the P.M. said that the government hopes to "Canadianize" the monarchy by
Speech from the Throne
quietly "depersonalizing" the Queen's role in favour of more emphasis on the constitutional position of the Governor General- by, for example, replacing the name of the Queen with that of the Governor General on all official documents.
It was said that this could not be in their minds. Then, the government came out later on with its organization of the government of Canada, a large volume that comes out each year. I venture the opinion that few of the members supporting the government have ever looked at it, and certainly we followed suit. It is simply a conglomeration of information. In January 1969, the statements in it followed the Provisions of the British North America Act. It stated:
The Executive Government and authority of and over Canada is hereby declared to continue and be vested in the Queen.
That has been erased. It now says that the cabinet is actually in charge of the executive. If you follow it along, you see what has happened. The Governor General cannot do anything except that which his ministers permit him to do. He is the representative of the Queen. He is not the leader of this nation. He is not a head of state. Yet, in
1971	he was in Iran at their twenty five hundredth anniversary. There were three categories of guests invited: royalty, heads of state and representatives of heads of state. The Governor General of Australia was in the third category, but the Governor General of Canada was there as a head of state.
The direction of the movement is obvious, but suddenly the Prime Minister changes his mind. His actions can almost be compared to those of Saul on the way to Damascus. After having criticized the monarchy, both directly and by imputation, the Prime Minister now in
1972	says that he will not abolish the monarchy. He has made a sudden discovery that he cannot do it. The only way in which the Crown can be abolished is by a vote of the House of Commons, the Senate and all the provinces. So, he comes out in his white shining armour and says "I am all for the Queen", and she gets triple mention in the 1972 Speech from the Throne, but there was no mention of her two years ago.
Now, I come to a matter that has been up several times, that is the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I have listened to what the Prime Minister said outside the House. I wish he would say some of those things in the House, and then I would operate without anaesthetic. Let him say them, even if he reads them, in the House of Commons. Why is there no reference to it being a detachment of the RCM police? Is this the result of policy?
I did not receive any reply on January 17. Yet, they had the answers. If the story they are telling today is true, why did they not give it? It took two telephone calls to prod them into giving an answer. This was before they worked out this latest alibi for what has been done. The answer stated:
I am informed that this detachment displays the new sign designed by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to blend with contemporary buildings.
That was the explanation, and it indicates, of course, that the sign was designed by the RCMP. They have to blame somebody. The explanation that was given to me tells the story of the falsity of what is endeavoured today to fool the Canadian people. I simply say through you, Sir, to the government of Canada: your conduct toward the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has lost you hundreds of thousands of votes, not only in western Canada but throughout Canada, and you cannot alibi yourselves out of that.

speechtext: What is this new force that has been set up?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

That is right. The description of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) is well taken. But it is interesting that the government did not know there was such a thing. On January 29 I directed a question to the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp). It was in connection with the civilian secret service being established to replace the RCMP security and intelligence agency. Finally, the former minister of manpower and immigration said there was nothing to that. Then, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) asked about it and received much the same answer. But the Prime Minister said:
Here again I think there is a misunderstanding. This is not a separate security force as the hon. member seemed to understand. It is a small co-ordinating body to make sure that the ministers in the cabinet have information collected from various sources including the RCMP so that the government will be better informed on the facts spread around in the various government departments.
Somebody asked the Prime Minister who was going to head it. He asked:
Who is going to head the non-force, Mr. Speaker, a non-head?
The person who answers to that description, of course, is the Solicitor General. Then, Douglas Fisher, an astute member of the press gallery and a one time member of parliament wrote:
I understand that the new departmental group is to have a permanent advisory function but that its first assignment is to recommend changes in the composition and operation of the RCMP.
They don't like the RCMP. As long as the RCMP is in charge, there is no danger in our country from communism. But it wasn't sufficient.
Then, the Solicitor General stepped in and explained away the unexplainable in these words, to be found at page 7699, and here he was quoting the Prime Minister:
The security service, under the Commissioner of the RCMP, will be increasingly separate in structure and civilian in nature.
In his own words, he said:
That principle remains. It is respected, and the fact that a research and planning group has been put in action does not change anything in the basic principle expressed by the Prime Minister.
I would add that there is no question of this group directing police operations as such. As a matter of fact, as is indicated by its name, it is a research group, a planning group that will be mainly concerned with analysis.
The black cat gets out of the bag in the next sentence.
In fact, what are the true responsibilities of this working group? First of all, to compile information and not to go and find it; also to set up some police services. The information will be provided mainly by the RCMP, of course, as well as by the Armed Forces, other departments that have information relating to the security of the country as well as by provincial government and other sources accessible to the public.
It should then assess this information and call for additional information should the data obtained be inadequate. Finally, it should analyse the information as a whole, not merely from a strict police point of view, but in a much wider spirit, that is taking into consideration social, economic and political factors.
February 29, 1972

That is where the truth gets out. This force that has been set up is investigating. It is a force away from the RCMP, and among other things it is supposed to look into political matters. When one thinks how that murderer was given such fine attention that he was able to escape from the penitentiary, one wonders whether that comes under the heading of a much wider spirit which is included in the phrase "social, economic and political factors."
The Prime Minister said it is not true. He said the big lie shocks him. If he were here today, I would deal with that question at length. The truth is that every person in this country who has looked at the new RCMP badge knows that the designation "Royal Canadian Mounted Police" is out, excepting for the coat of arms. And the reason given is that the people, when they are looking for the police, do not know what RCMP means. That is what the Prime Minister said the other day. He said, "It is false. We have not done anything."
I have here a picture from the Toronto Star, Mr. Speaker. I cannot put it on the Hansard record; I wish I could. It shows the Solicitor General looking at a sign. This is the sign with the Coat of Arms and "Police." There is nothing else. What is being done in this case is undermining the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and then the government explains it by saying the Royal Canadian Mounted Police thought they would like the change made. Can the Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police say that? A few months ago he pointed out that if an embassy were opened in Ottawa by China, it would be a breeding place for agitators. He was immediately told, "Shut your mouth and never talk again." Yet now, these same people come along and, to exculpate themselves with respect to the dastardly deed that has been committed, they say, "After all, the Mounted Police wanted it done."

Now, Sir, I will move away from Canada to the international field, but only for a short time. I do not think I have ever known my country to be lower in prestige internationally than it is today. The statement by the Prime Minister that we feared the United States militarily was one that shocked the sensibilities not only of Americans but of free men everywhere in the world.
Then, there was the other statement made by the Prime Minister when he was asked by Ukrainian Canadians, and Ukrainians from other parts of the world, to bring to the attention of the Soviet authorities what was taking place today, not only in the Ukraine but throughout the captive nations of the world. Kosygin, when he was here, said he loved peace. How he must have laughed when he said that. Today Brezhnev and Kosygin are reviving the Stali-
Speech from the Throne
nist repression that seemed to end with the elevation of Khrushchev to authority.
In the case of the Ukrainian people, 11 of their leaders have been arrested, not because of their advocacy of revolution but because they have been critical of the Soviet government's failure to live up to its pledged principles in the United Nations. There is a new wave of Russian persecutions against Ukrainians. The intellectuals who speak out are accused of dealing in anti-Soviet propaganda. The Sovier courts are applying a new rule and imposing additional sentences for acts allegedly committed against Soviet society while an accused is in prison. I can give example after example. One is Valentyn Moroz, a young Hungarian historian, who was sentenced in 1970 to nine years of hard labour for writing a report about Beria Reserve while serving a previous sentence of four years in that prison camp. I have the list here of free men, many of them communists, who are being put in jail without trial.
The World Congress of Free Ukrainians wishes to have this matter fully investigated. I intend to do what I can in that connection, it having honoured me by naming me as the national chairman. I will do what I can to assure those who love freedom, as we love freedom, in the Ukraine and in the Baltic countries of Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia, and in other countries that are under communist domination, that what is wrong will be revealed.
People ask where does the Prime Minister come in on this? I do not want to quote at length, but I will quote what he said when he was asked by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) what he was going to do about it, and what he had done. As reported on May 31 he said he had little sympathy with nationalists in Canada or the Soviet Union. He said:
I quite frankly avoided talking about that. I tried to get some data which would permit me to talk about it on a basis on which I felt really involved and convinced, and-quite frankly-couldn't take up the causes, several of which were put to me, that I should protest in favour of so-and-so and so-and-so who had been jailed because of their nationalistic beliefs.
My position in the Soviet Union or in Canada is that anyone who breaks the law to assert his nationalism does not get too much sympathy from me.
In 1958, he said that everyone had the right to oppose any law if he did not agree with it.
Again, according to the report on May 31, he said:
I didn't particularly feel like bringing up any cases which would have caused Mr. Brezhnev or Mr. Kosygin to say: 'Well you know, why did you put in jail certain FLQ leaders? After all they think they are only fighting for the independence of Quebec. Our people say they are fighting for the independence of the Ukraine. Why should you put your revolutionaries in jail and we shouldn't put ours?
That statement was an insult to every Canadian of Ukrainian origin and to every other Canadian.

It is equating the murderers and kidnappers with intellectuals who are simply advocating that the law be lived up to. Then, when the Prime Minister got into difficulty about that he said "I really didn't mean that". The same old equivocal course. Say the thing, have

February 29, 1972
Speech from the Throne
the accolade of Kosygin placed upon the brow for having said it, then say "I really didn't mean it". If I say that he must have meant it somebody might say that I have partisan reasons, but I will quote from the Winnipeg Free Press of June 2, 1971. This newspaper is an avowed and dedicated supporter of the Liberal party but an article in it reads:
Prime Minister Trudeau's unfortunate comparison between the Ukrainian nationalists and the FLQ in Quebec is beyond comprehension.
And later, in the same article:
The Ukrainian nationalists were arrested because they strove to keep alive Ukrainian culture, language and literature in an increasingly Russian environment.
Perhaps the Prime Minister has forgotten the millions of dollars spent on the B and B commission for an analogous performance if he is really seeking analogies. Then, in the same article:
To compare these Ukrainian martyrs with a misguided band of kidnappers and assassins is not only an insult to the Ukrainian intellectuals and their kin, but a slap in the face of every democrat who abhors totalitarian tyranny.
Having got himself in that difficulty, he followed his usual course. He brought the leaders of the Canadian Ukrainian Committee to Ottawa and told them that he loved them, that what he said was misunderstood. But no amount of charisma can explain away what took place when he dared say this to people with that little flame of freedom before them. Many of them were martyred. Today thousands are in danger and hundreds have been picked up recently. Why has the Canadian government not pointed this out at the United Nations? They have never said a word, not one word. When Khrushchev was there in September, 1960, I mentioned the awfulness of the course of these people, and I was told by the highest ecclesiastics that the change that took place thereafter was amazing because public opinion in every other part of the world does affect the Soviet Union. This country has half a million Ukrainians, some of whom are our finest citizens and have served our country tremendously in days of war as they served in peace. It is beyond me to contemplate why the Prime Minister should have engaged in the blackmail of untruth.
I told you, Your Honour, that I would only take a few minutes. I thank the House for its consideration in permitting me extra time.
